hints: Express the resistance unit through the potential-difference–current relationship.
Use resistance as potential difference divided by current.
State the resistance corresponding to 1 V across a component when 1 A flows.
walkthrough: Resistance is measured as potential difference divided by current, so its unit is volt per ampere.
A component has resistance 1 Ω when a potential difference of 1 V produces a current of 1 A.

ai_rubric.observable: Defines the ohm as volt per ampere, or as the resistance for which 1 V produces 1 A.

hints: Start with the relation between resistance, resistivity, length and cross-sectional area.
Use the constant volume to write the cross-sectional area in terms of the wire length.
Substitute for area, then identify the quantities that remain constant.
walkthrough: For a uniform wire, R = ρL / A.
Its constant volume is V = AL, so A = V / L.
Substituting gives R = ρL / (V / L) = ρL² / V.
As ρ and V are constant, R is proportional to L².

ai_rubric.observable: Uses R = ρL / A for the wire.
Uses A = V / L and derives R = ρL² / V, then states that R ∝ L² because resistivity and volume are constant.

hints: The graph shows terminal potential difference V against current I.
At zero current, there is no potential difference lost across the battery's internal resistance.
Read the V-axis intercept, where I = 0.
walkthrough: For a battery supplying current, V = ℰ − Ir.
At I = 0, the internal voltage loss Ir is zero, so V equals the e.m.f. ℰ.
The V-axis intercept on the graph is 2.4 V.

ai_rubric.observable: Reads the e.m.f. as 2.4 V from the V-axis intercept at zero current.

hints: First read the potential difference across the variable resistor at I = 5.0 A from the graph.
Choose a power relationship that uses the current and potential difference across that same resistor.
Multiply the graph reading by 5.0 A and give the result in watts.
walkthrough: At I = 5.0 A, the graph gives V = 1.3 V across the variable resistor.
Use P = VI for the resistor.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses an accepted electrical-power relationship, such as P = VI, P = I²R or P = V²/R.
Uses consistent graph-derived values, for example 1.3 V and 5.0 A.

hints: Compare the straight-line graph with the terminal-potential-difference equation.
In V = ℰ − Ir, identify the coefficient of I.
Remember that the graph descends, so its gradient is negative.
walkthrough: The source relationship is V = ℰ − Ir.
On a graph of V against I, the gradient is −r.
Therefore the magnitude of the gradient represents the internal resistance r of the battery.

ai_rubric.observable: States that the negative gradient represents the internal resistance r of the battery.
